candidate.answerReason: On the original logarithm domain, the product on the left equals \(\log_3 y\), while the right side equals \(2\). Hence \(y=9\), agreeing with choice B.

methods.label: Method 1: Change to a common base
methods.explanation:
Using one common base makes the intermediate logarithms cancel. First, the original logarithms require
\[
x>0,\qquad x\ne1,\qquad x\ne\frac12,\qquad y>0.
\]
These conditions ensure that \(\log_{10}x\) and \(\log_{10}(2x)\) are nonzero. By the change of base formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
& (\log_3x)(\log_x(2x))(\log_{2x}y)\\
&\quad=\frac{\log_{10}x}{\log_{10}3}
\cdot\frac{\log_{10}(2x)}{\log_{10}x}
\cdot\frac{\log_{10}y}{\log_{10}(2x)}\\
&\quad=\frac{\log_{10}y}{\log_{10}3}
=\log_3y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Also, \(\log_x(x^2)=2\), because raising the valid base \(x\) to the second power gives \(x^2\). The equation therefore becomes \(\log_3y=2\), so
\[
y=3^2=\boxed{9}.
\]
This positive value satisfies the simplified equation, and all preceding transformations are valid on the original domain. The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: Change of base, logarithm domains, and conversion between logarithmic and exponential statements are permitted high-school precalculus.

methods.label: Method 2: Read the logarithms as exponents
methods.explanation:
The successive bases \(3,x,2x\) form a chain, so we can interpret each logarithm as an exponent. The original domain is
\[
x>0,\qquad x\ne1,\qquad x\ne\frac12,\qquad y>0.
\]
Set
\[
p=\log_3x,\qquad q=\log_x(2x),\qquad r=\log_{2x}y.
\]
By the definition of a logarithm,
\[
x=3^p,\qquad 2x=x^q,\qquad y=(2x)^r.
\]
All bases are positive, so the power-of-a-power law gives
\[
y=(x^q)^r=x^{qr}=(3^p)^{qr}=3^{pqr}.
\]
The given equation says \(pqr=\log_x(x^2)=2\). Hence \(y=3^2=\boxed{9}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\). The same identities show that this value works for every allowed \(x\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses only the definition of logarithms and real exponent laws for positive bases, within high-school precalculus.
